newsitem.title: JAPAN: Iraqi oil seen competing with Iran crude in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi oil seen competing with Iran crude in Asia.

text.p: The return of Iraqi crude oil to the global market after an absence of six years could undermine sales of Iranian Light crude in Asia in the long term, industry sources in Tokyo said on Thursday.
However, they said that the immediate impact from Iraqi crude oil would be marginal given the limited volumes Baghdad was being allowed to export under the United Nations oil-for-food deal.

Under the plan implemented on December 10, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food and medicine for its people, suffering under sanctions imposed in August 1990 when Iraq invaded Kuwait.
Industry sources said a number of Japanese refineries were designed to use Arabian Light as their main grade of crude oil.
Basrah Light -- the crude grade that Mitsubishi Corp last week agreed to buy from Iraq -- shares more similar qualities with Arabian Light than Iranian Light.
Given the same economics and the chance, some refineries would probably shift to using Basrah Light from Iranian Light if Iraq made a full return to global markets, traders said.
The Iranian crude has a relatively high content of nitrogen and heavy metals, materials which can put a strain on the catalyst used in some Japanese secondary refining systems.
"There are some Japanese refineries that are using the (Iranian) crude despite the strain (on their systems)," one oil trader said.
Mitsubishi signed a deal to buy 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil over three months from Iraq. The contract, the first concluded by a Japanese firm, is now awaiting U.N. approval.
The major trading company is acting for five Japanese oil companies which will be lifting crude from the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr.

The Asian crude spot market has so far largely shrugged off the extra barrels of Iraqi crude that will soon be heading to East Asia. This is partly because the volume that has been contracted so far is only about one-fifth of the roughly 200,000 bpd that Japan used to import from Iraq before U.N. sanctions.

Moreover, under the terms of the contract, Iraq will only sell the crude if the name of the company which is the final consumer of the oil is provided. This means none of it will be traded on the spot market.
"It's not much compared to what used to come to Japan, and the Iraqi crude will go into the systems of the (Japanese) refineries," one crude trader said.
Oman is a competing crude of a similar grade as Basrah Light that is traded on the spot market and was most likely to be undermined by resumption of Iraqi crude exports, traders said.
However, premiums for February cargoes of Oman -- the most actively traded month -- have risen on tight physical supplies.
Regarding Asia as a whole, traders in Singapore said China currently could not run Iraqi crude because of its high sulphur content.
They said this was expected to be a major factor affecting the impact of Iraqi crude on Asian supply and demand.
"China can't run Iraqi crude because it is too high in sulphur," said one trader. "So our biggest swing buyer cannot take Iraq crude."
